ideas.title: The teleprompter operator's trading account
ideas.hook: The man who loads Trump's teleprompter made a hundred grand betting on what Trump would say.
ideas.why: This is insider trading, except the inside information is a script. Gabriel Perez had run the president's teleprompter since 2016, which meant he knew the prepared remarks before anyone else — and Kalshi runs "mention markets," contracts that pay out on whether a specific word gets said. He bet on more than a dozen speeches, including the State of the Union. The detail that makes it a video rather than a headline: nobody tipped off the government. Kalshi's own surveillance system flagged the betting pattern as anomalous, and only then did investigators notice the account belonged to a federal employee. The exchange caught it the way an exchange catches things.

beats.text: The job title, then the number. Nothing else.
What a mention market is: a contract that pays $1 if the word gets said. Perez had the script.
How he got caught — Kalshi's surveillance flagged the pattern, not a whistleblower. That is the tell that this is market infrastructure, not a casino.
On August 13 the CFTC opened a review of mention markets generally. Kalshi pulled the sports ones. The Trump and earnings-call markets are still live.

ideas.title: Six grid operators, one deadline
ideas.hook: On Monday, six companies have to explain why your power bill should pay for a data center.
ideas.why: There is a clock on this one and almost nobody outside energy law is watching it. On June 18 FERC issued Section 206 show-cause orders to all six US grid operators at once — PJM, MISO, SPP, CAISO, ISO-NE and NYISO — and did something unusual: it declared their existing tariffs for large loads presumptively unjust. That flips the burden. Normally a regulator has to prove a rule is broken; here the operators have 60 days to prove theirs isn't. Sixty days from June 18 is August 17. The specific question they have to answer is who pays for the substations and transmission when a 20-megawatt-plus load shows up, and the honest answer for the last two years has been "everyone else's bill."

beats.text: The deadline and what is being asked.
Six orders, six dockets, one day. The threshold is 20 MW. A large data center is many multiples of that.
What "presumptively unjust" means: FERC did not ask them to consider a change, it put the burden of proof on them to defend the status quo.
Watch what actually gets filed Monday. A defence means your bill keeps absorbing it; a reform filing means the data centers start paying their own interconnection costs.

sources.name: FERC, the announcement
McGuireWoods, dockets EL26-67 through EL26-72 and the section 206 mechanics

ideas.saturation: low — covered thoroughly by energy trade press, essentially not at all for a general audience

ideas.title: DeepSeek raises prices tenfold
ideas.hook: The cheap AI just got ten times more expensive. The expensive ones got cheaper.
ideas.why: The whole story of the last two years was that Chinese labs would drive the price of a token to zero. This week it inverted. DeepSeek notified developers on August 6 of a significant price rise and has raised some V4 pricing by more than tenfold, while OpenAI and Anthropic cut prices on selected models. The reason is the interesting part: DeepSeek won on price, demand went to roughly seven trillion tokens a week, and it cannot buy its way out of the squeeze because it cannot freely buy more chips. The US labs cut prices because they have compute. So the price on the invoice was never really about model efficiency — it was about who can add capacity.

beats.text: The inversion, stated flatly.
August 6 notice, some V4 prices up more than 10x. OpenAI and Anthropic moving the other way.
Why: demand hit ~7 trillion tokens a week against a fixed fleet. Price is the only lever left when you cannot add GPUs.
The thing to carry: a token price is a compute-access price wearing a software costume. Watch whether the cuts on the US side survive the memory and power squeeze.

ideas.title: Build a video pipeline once
ideas.hook: I built this shot once. Then I made forty more without touching it again.

beats.text: Ten finished clips in a grid. They all match.
Back to one node graph. This is the entire thing.
Build it live: extract, mask, colour match, image-to-video. Every layer stays editable, unlike a single text prompt.
Swap the input, run again. The pipeline is the asset, not the output.

sources.name: Figma, node-based AI video compositing
Weave subscription plans and credit caps

ideas.saturation: low — plenty of "look, AI video" content, almost none on reusable pipelines

extra.What you build: A reusable node graph in Figma Weave that takes a still image and runs it through the same extract, mask, colour-match and animate chain every time — then you drop in ten different images and get ten consistent clips out.
extra.Time to build: 30-40 minutes for the first graph, seconds per asset after that
extra.The money shot: The graph itself, running. Every compositing step is a visible node, so you can pull one out on camera and watch the output change — and then the batch: the same pipeline chewing through a folder of stills and producing clips that actually match each other. Consistency at volume is the thing AI video is worst at, so showing it is the whole video.
extra.Gotchas: Weave bills separately from Figma — Figma credits and Weave credits do not transfer, and a paid Figma plan does not include Weave. The free tier is 150 credits a month capped at 5 workflows, which is enough to film this but not enough to work in; Starter is $24/month. Weave tools inside Figma Design are free during open beta for paid Figma subscribers, which is worth saying on screen because it will not stay that way.

ideas.title: An agent that reads X
ideas.hook: No API key. No login. Watch it pull a profile in about four seconds.

beats.text: One command in a bare terminal. Real data comes back.
Add it to Claude as an MCP server. Four lines of config.
Ask for something a human would hate doing: read these fifteen accounts, tell me what is actually new.
The honest boundary — this is for reading, not for auto-posting. Say why you are not showing the follow bots.

sources.name: XActions repo, MCP config and the no-auth demo

extra.What you build: XActions wired into Claude as an MCP server, so an agent can read X — profiles, timelines, search — and hand you a written brief instead of you scrolling for forty minutes.
extra.The money shot: Open with the thirty-second proof, on camera, before any setup: `npx xactions profile nasa` and real data comes back. No account, no key, no browser. Then the actual payoff — the agent reads a list of accounts and writes you a morning brief, and you show the brief next to the raw timeline it replaced.
extra.Gotchas: The repo is active (commits through August 4, 53 CLI commands, MCP server) and most read functions genuinely need no auth, but logging in unlocks search, followers and DMs. It also ships engagement-automation features — follow bots, auto-like — that will get an account actioned and are not what this video is about. Draw that line out loud or the comments will be about nothing else.

ideas.title: Memory your coding agent can't fake
ideas.hook: I renamed a function last week. Watch my agent confidently tell me the old name.

beats.text: The wrong answer, delivered confidently.
Why: agent memory is usually a text file that nothing ever re-checks.
`npx -y @kage-core/kage-graph-mcp install`. It builds a code graph and wires itself into the agent.
Same question, correct answer. Then the part that matters for teams: it is committed to the repo, so it travels through git.

sources.name: Kage repo
Project site

extra.What you build: Kage — persistent memory for a coding agent that lives in your repo as plain Markdown and gets checked against the actual code before it is ever served back.
extra.The money shot: Set a trap and spring it on camera. Rename something, wait for the agent's memory file to go stale, then ask about it — it answers confidently and wrongly. Install Kage, ask again, and the stale memory does not come back, because the memory was validated against the code and failed. The falsifiable version of "agent memory" is the video: most memory tools cannot show you this because they cannot detect the staleness in the first place.
extra.Gotchas: Early — 32 stars, though 766 commits and 340+ tests behind it, so it is real work rather than a weekend wrapper. GPL-3.0 (earlier releases were MIT), which matters if you are putting it in a commercial repo. Node 18+, no account, no API key, no database. Cloud tier is waitlisted; do not build the video around it.

ideas.title: A data center is a heater
ideas.hook: A data center converts almost one hundred percent of its electricity into heat. The thinking is a side effect.

beats.text: The claim, flat.
Follow one watt in. Show where it can possibly go. There is nowhere else.
So cooling is not a tax on the power bill, it is the second half of the same watt. That is why siting is really about water and air, not land.
Pairs to the news: this is what the grid operators are actually arguing about on Monday.

sources.name: IEEE, thermodynamics of IT data centers
TechRadar, the AI heat trap

extra.The misconception: That a data center uses electricity to do computing, and cooling is an unfortunate side cost on top. It is closer to the reverse: essentially all the electricity becomes heat, and the computing is something that happens on the way.
extra.The analogy: An electric space heater is 100% efficient by definition — every watt in becomes a watt of heat out. A data center is the same device with better manners. Nothing leaves the building as "computation"; a rounding error leaves as light down a fibre. The rest leaves as warm air, which is why cooling is not overhead sitting beside the power bill — it is the same watt showing up on the bill a second time.
extra.Where the analogy breaks: It does not tell you computing is wasteful. The physical floor for erasing a bit is real but is roughly a billion times below what actual chips use, so thermodynamics is not the binding constraint — engineering is. And the heat is not always wasted: some sites now sell it into district heating, which is the one case where the space-heater framing becomes literally the business model.
extra.Pairs with: A2 — film them back to back.

ideas.title: Why long chats get expensive

beats.text: The reframe: it re-reads everything, every time.
The handshake table. Draw it growing.
Why you feel it: the long thread that got slow, the API bill that grew faster than the transcript.
Then the honest correction — caching. And the reason that matters this week is that compute scarcity is now showing up directly in prices.

sources.name: DigitalOcean, long-context inference cost in production
FastKV, prefill and KV-cache costs

ideas.saturation: medium — widely explained, rarely with the caching correction attached, which is the part that makes it honest

extra.The misconception: That a model reads your message once, the way you read a message once. It re-reads the entire conversation from the beginning to produce every single word it says back.
extra.The analogy: A dinner party where, before anyone speaks, every guest has to shake hands with every other guest. Ten guests is manageable. A hundred guests is not ten times worse, it is a hundred times worse — the handshakes grow with the square of the table. That is attention. Each new token has to consult every token before it, so the cost of a conversation does not grow with its length, it grows with the square of its length.
extra.Where the analogy breaks: Real systems cheat, legitimately. The key-value cache means the model does not literally redo every handshake for every new word — earlier work is stored and reused, which pulls the per-token cost down to linear. Prompt caching goes further and is the one optimisation that gets cheaper the longer the context runs. So the honest version is: the quadratic term is real and it is why long context was hard, but the industry has spent three years building machinery specifically to avoid paying it.

ideas.title: The digit that catches fraud

beats.text: Fake numbers do not look random enough. That is how they get caught.
The 30.1% / 4.6% split. Show the curve.
Why it happens: percentage growth spends longer in the low digits. The 1,000-to-2,000 versus 9,000-to-10,000 image.

Where it fails, and the live example — Jefferies was told this month that invoices behind its financing to an iron ore trader were not genuine, which is exactly the shape of data this test is built for.

sources.name: ACFE, why fraud examiners use it
Significance (Royal Statistical Society), detecting the dubious digits
Benford's law, distribution and limits
Bloomberg, the Jefferies fake-invoice story

ideas.saturation: medium — the law is well covered, the "too evenly spread" framing and the honest limits usually are not

extra.The misconception: That made-up numbers look random, and that looking random is what makes them convincing. It is the opposite — real-world numbers are lopsided in a very specific way, and fabricated ones are usually too evenly spread.
extra.The analogy: Watch a number grow by percentages instead of by addition. To climb from 1,000 to 2,000 it has to gain 100%, so it spends a long time starting with a 1. To get from 9,000 to 10,000 it needs only 11%, so it barely pauses on 9. Anything that grows this way — invoices, populations, river lengths, expenses — piles up on the low digits. First digit 1 shows up about 30.1% of the time. Digit 9 shows up about 4.6%. A fraudster inventing invoices reaches for 800 and 900 because they want the money, and flattens the curve.
extra.Where the analogy breaks: It is a red flag, not a verdict, and it fails cleanly in predictable places: numbers with hard floors and ceilings, assigned numbers like ZIP codes, and prices deliberately set at $9.99. It also cannot catch a single theft — it needs a population of numbers to test. Courts in the US do accept it, but as one tool among several, never as proof on its own. The honest ending is that Benford's law tells you where to look, and then a human still has to go look.

ideas.title: The rating nobody was meant to read
ideas.hook: There is a credit rating agency with about twenty analysts that graded more than three thousand private credit investments in a single year. US insurers are holding roughly forty billion dollars of debt it graded. And you cannot read a single one of those ratings, because they were never published. They were never meant to be.
ideas.why: Private letter ratings did not inflate because someone was tricking investors — there are no investors reading them. They inflated because the only audience is a regulatory capital formula, and the company buying the rating is the same company the rating lets hold less capital.

beats.text: Twenty analysts, three thousand ratings, forty billion dollars, zero published pages. Sit on the arithmetic.
What a private letter rating is and why it exists at all: insurers must hold capital against what they own, and how much depends on a letter grade. No grade, no cheap capital.

Act one, the story you think this is. Egan-Jones: two former executives suing, alleging they were fired after raising conflicts with regulators; an SEC probe into its ratings practices; Bermuda quietly removing it from the recognised-ratings list in January. The firm denies all of it.

Act two, the turn. These ratings are unpublished — there is no investor to defraud. The audience is a formula. Then the NAIC's own numbers: 106 of 109 above its analysts' assessment, six notches, an 84% capital reduction. And the agency that found it pulled its own report.

Act three, follow it offshore. Roughly two trillion dollars of US life liabilities ceded to offshore and captive reinsurers; Bermuda's long-term reinsurers holding $1.52 trillion, over 80% of it originating in the US. The privately graded paper backs retirement annuities, and it is increasingly not in the country that sold them.

The turn to now: Actuarial Guideline 55, adopted this month, extends asset adequacy testing to reinsured blocks for the first time; Treasury Secretary Bessent has met state regulators about it. Then the honest uncertainty — none of this has broken. Defaults are low. The open question is not whether the number was a lie, it is whether the number was ever measuring anything.

ideas.note: verify the six-notch and 84% figures against the NAIC report text before filming —

extra.Why it holds ten minutes: It has a real turn in the middle. The first three minutes look exactly like a 2008 rerun — a small agency, fees for grades, a whistleblower suit — and the viewer arrives already knowing this story. Then the second act takes it away from them: these ratings are unpublished, so the usual fraud framing does not fit. The back half brings in material almost no coverage uses: the NAIC's own 2024 study, which sampled 109 private letter ratings and found 106 of them rated higher than the NAIC's own analysts assessed — 17 of them investment-grade on paper while the NAIC read them as junk, some inflated by six notches. Then the arithmetic that makes it worth doing: moving a credit six notches, from single-B to triple-B, cuts a life insurer's pre-tax risk-based capital charge by roughly 84%. Then the detail that turns it from a finance story into something worse: the NAIC pulled that report off its own website in May 2025 to "clarify" its findings, after industry pushback, and has never republished it. The third act follows the money offshore, and the last two minutes are genuinely live — the NAIC adopted Actuarial Guideline 55 this month.
extra.What you'd need: The Warren letter to Sean Egan (July 2025) on screen as a PDF — it is public and it names the conflict directly. The NAIC private letter ratings report is the best visual in the piece precisely because it is gone: show the citation, then the absence. A risk-based capital factor table with the single-B and triple-B rows highlighted, so the 84% is arithmetic the viewer watches rather than a claim they take. The Bermuda Monetary Authority recognised-ratings list before and after January. A Bermuda company registry page for a named life reinsurer. A plain annuity statement to close on — the object at the end of the chain.
extra.Thumbnail: A single page of a credit rating with everything redacted except an investment-grade letter grade in the corner. One subject, readable at any size.
